narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 63.2% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) for your year-three grades, far below the average of roughly the sixth decile among students who were accepted. This low academic standing in later law school years signaled to the model a higher risk of struggling with the bar exam.

Your undergraduate GPA came next in importance, but worked in the opposite direction. At 3.00 it was only modestly below the 3.23 average of accepted students, giving the model a mild reason to expect you might still pass.

Your LSAT score of 25.5 was the third most influential factor and pulled the prediction back toward failure. It sits well below the 37.2 average of accepted applicants, reinforcing the concern raised by your class rank.

Taken together, the model concluded that your academic performance trajectory and entrance exam results indicated a greater than 60% likelihood of not passing the bar on the first try.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retake the LSAT to raise your score, and consider additional bar-prep coursework or a structured study program that can demonstrably improve your command of the tested material before reapplying.
